query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor (~5 at%) addition of a ductilizing element (e.g., Ti) into equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW will promote the in situ formation of a dual‐phase microstructure at room temperature—comprising a continuous, disordered BCC matrix with coherent, nanoscale precipitates—that enhances ductility and acts as effective defect sinks under irradiation, while at temperatures above ~800 °C the precipitates dissolve or coarsen to restore a homogeneous BCC phase with excellent high‐temperature strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW that offers outstanding high-temperature mechanical performance (up to 1600 °C) but exhibits poor room-temperature ductility and only computationally inferred irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 atomic percent of Ti during the alloy synthesis via vacuum arc melting to enable controlled nano-precipitate formation, followed by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to stabilize the duplex microstructure at room temperature.
generation.conditions: Room temperature (for ductility and irradiation tests) and high temperatures above 800 °C (to assess reversion to single-phase BCC). Irradiation conditions such as helium ion implantation at moderate doses can be used to simulate irradiation environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-phase microstructure where a ductile, disordered BCC matrix coexists with coherent, nanoscale ductilizing precipitates that serve as defect sinks.
generation.mechanism: The Ti addition introduces local lattice distortions that favour the nucleation of fine precipitates during solidification and subsequent heat treatment. At room temperature, these precipitates disrupt crack propagation and enhance dislocation mobility, thereby improving ductility, while their interfaces serve as recombination centers for irradiation‐induced point defects. Upon heating above ~800 °C, the precipitates coarsen or dissolve, merging with the matrix to maintain the desirable high-temperature BCC strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to undoped NbMoTaW, the Ti-doped alloy is expected to show significantly increased room-temperature ductility (e.g., >20% improvement in fracture strain) and enhanced resistance to irradiation damage (evidenced by lower defect densities and reduced blistering) while preserving the high-temperature phase stability and strength of the original BCC structure.
generation.baseline: Undoped equiatomic NbMoTaW, which exhibits excellent high-temperature properties but poor room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance inferred only from computational studies.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated under standard room-temperature mechanical loading and moderate irradiation doses, with high-temperature performance evaluated above 800 °C. Excessive microalloying or processing-induced secondary phases beyond the limited volume fraction can compromise the intended balance.
generation.uncertainty: Precise control over the Ti content and processing parameters is required to achieve the targeted nano-precipitate morphology. The exact kinetics of precipitate dissolution at high temperature and their influence on irradiation defect recombination are not fully quantified, and there is uncertainty in balancing improved ductility with maintaining high-temperature strength.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys using identical processing conditions: one set of baseline NbMoTaW and another with an added 5 at% Ti. Apply a controlled thermo-mechanical treatment designed to induce and stabilize a duplex microstructure in the Ti-doped samples. Evaluate both sets via room-temperature tensile tests, irradiation exposure (e.g., helium ion implantations), and high-temperature mechanical tests (above 800 °C). Microstructural evaluations using TEM/SEM and phase analysis using XRD should be conducted pre- and post-treatment.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile ductility (fracture strain, elongation), yield strength, and fracture toughness.
TEM/SEM for precipitate size, distribution, and coherence with the matrix.
Post-irradiation defect characterization (defect density, blistering, amorphization) via TEM and relevant diffraction techniques.
High-temperature phase analysis (XRD) and mechanical testing (compressive/tensile strength) above 800 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped NbMoTaW does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., less than a 20% increase in fracture strain) or fails to display a reduced irradiation-induced defect density compared to the undoped alloy—and if its high-temperature performance degrades or remains unchanged—the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Question: Can a quaternary tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) exhibit superior radiation resistance compared to pure tungsten, specifically regarding the formation of dislocation loops under fusion-relevant irradiation conditions?. System: Quaternary W-Ta-V-Cr high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V. Processing: Magnetron sputtering deposition from pure metal targets (99.99% purity) using powers of 192 W (Cr), 312 W (V), 277 W (Ta), and 300 W (W) at 3 mtorr pressure and room temperature; films deposited on NaCl (100 nm) or Si (3 μm) substrates.
